key_finding: A state-of-the-art review of DC plan design covering auto-enrollment, default investment options, and their short- and long-term effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative overview of academic and industry literature on defined-contribution plan design (abstract-only).
why_it_matters: Gives a broad synthesis of what's known about default and engagement effects in retirement plans, a useful baseline for comparison even though it doesn't address consumer fintech settings directly.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan setting, not consumer self-directed
no quantitative effect sizes given in abstract
relevance_reason: Broad recent review of default/auto-enrollment effects and disengagement, useful context from the adjacent employer-plan literature the brief treats as analogy only.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation, and only 40% of people with an auto-escalation default actually escalate on the first date, with more opting out later.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job turnover, unvested matches, withdrawal upon separation, and auto-escalation opt-out.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's objection that defaults' apparent enrolment lift is much smaller in steady state than short-run figures suggest, once real-world attrition and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: 401(k) employer retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings app
no evidence on round-up-style micro-savings products specifically
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with quantified medium/long-run erosion of the default effect.

key_finding: Shrouding the credit-card autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months, but did not significantly reduce debt because nudged cardholders picked autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Field experiment on credit-card autopay enrollment with six-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt outcomes.
why_it_matters: Shows a default-style nudge can shift nominal behavior while anchoring people just above a floor and failing to move the outcome that matters (debt/savings amount) — a direct caution for a preset multiplier and for treating enrolment numbers as success.
limitations: credit-card debt paydown context, not a savings product
does not directly test opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrolment designs
relevance_reason: Consumer financial field experiment showing a default shifts behavior nominally without changing the real financial outcome, directly bearing on the amount-vs-enrolment and anchoring questions.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most people who preferred otherwise actively opted out, and the default effect was strongest under high incentives, complex choices, and low awareness of enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using nationwide administrative and survey data around Germany's auto-enrollment rollout.
why_it_matters: Quantifies the opt-in vs opt-out default effect size and shows it is moderated by incentive strength, choice complexity, and awareness — directly relevant to predicting whether our round-up default will be seen as helpful or simply reversed.
limitations: public pension enrollment, not a consumer fintech product
no experimental active-choice condition, inferred only from opt-out rates
relevance_reason: Directly compares opt-in/opt-out default effects with a quantified size and heterogeneity, closely analogous to the entry-design decision.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions at 12 months is substantially attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings gains at that horizon (though inequality in savings falls), and a life-cycle model estimates a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Provides a recent, rigorous quantification of exactly the 'does the default effect persist at 6-12+ months' question the brief asks, even though set in employer retirement plans.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings app
36-month horizon still longer than typical liquid-savings usage patterns in an app
relevance_reason: Best available recent quantification of default-effect attenuation over time, directly informing the persistence question even from an adjacent setting.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment boosts short-term participation but induces long-term passivity (low contribution rates, inactive management, account churn), so participation alone doesn't prove welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy discussion synthesizing prior empirical findings; no new data (abstract-only).
why_it_matters: Articulates the exact enrolment-vs-passivity trade-off the brief poses and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment prompts) that could translate to round-up multiplier design.
limitations: employer 401(k) context
narrative/opinion piece without original data or effect sizes
very low citation count and unclear rigor
relevance_reason: Frames the enrolment-vs-passivity trade-off central to the brief, though as a qualitative essay in the employer-plan literature.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-European-country experiment (n=4207), default nudges shifted risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but also lowered ratings of the advisor's advice, especially when the default was refused, and how the default was framed shifted the amount invested.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country online experiment testing default presence, framing, and risk-taking outcomes.
why_it_matters: Directly informs both open decisions: shows defaults strongly move the level people end up at (relevant to preset-multiplier anchoring) and gives EU-based evidence that imposing or refusing a default lowers perceived trustworthiness — a direct signal of dark-pattern risk.
limitations: investment/wealth-management risk-taking context rather than a round-up savings feature
no 6-12 month persistence data
relevance_reason: EU experimental evidence on default framing's effect on chosen level and on perceived manipulativeness, directly actionable for both open design decisions.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still anchored there after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms with automatic enrollment, tracked over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that default enrolment anchors people at the preset level rather than freeing optimal choice — the foundational evidence behind the concern that a preset multiplier will anchor most users regardless of what they'd otherwise pick.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, predating today's fintech/app context and EU regulatory climate
an older foundational study the brief flags as superseded by newer work
relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring evidence that current literature (e.g., Choukhmane 2025, Choi et al. 2024) directly argues with.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence comes from the interaction of a preference-deviation cost and an opt-out effort cost, and that adding a 15% tip option to the existing menu captures 69% of achievable welfare gains at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transaction data plus a stated-preference survey identifying preferences independently of defaults.
why_it_matters: Gives a mechanism-level account of how preset menu options anchor consumer choice, directly relevant to deciding which multiplier to preselect and how many presets to offer, though the domain is tipping rather than financial savings.
limitations: studies tipping decisions, not a financial savings product
consumer setting differs substantially from a banking/savings app
relevance_reason: Rich mechanism-based evidence on how preset default menus anchor consumer choice, a useful methodological analogy for the multiplier-preset decision.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and theoretical framework for when and how default choice architecture produces downstream effects on consumer behavior, identifying antecedent preferences, timing of choice/consumption, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing prior default-effects literature into a framework and research agenda (abstract-only, no new empirical data).
why_it_matters: Offers a framework for what to measure and watch for regarding downstream disengagement after default enrollment, informing how we design 6-12 month follow-up measurement rather than the enrolment design itself.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual paper without new empirical effect sizes
not specific to financial products or fintech
relevance_reason: Provides a conceptual framework for anticipating and measuring downstream default effects like disengagement, useful for post-launch monitoring design.

key_finding: Derives a general theoretical characterization of when opt-out-minimizing versus maximizing default options are asymptotically optimal, extending prior restrictive-condition results and verifying accuracy via simulation.
methodology: Theoretical/computational economic modeling of optimal default design with asymptotic approximations verified by simulation.
why_it_matters: Offers abstract normative principles about default design (e.g., minimizing opt-out is near-optimal when designer and chooser agree) but no empirical effect sizes or consumer-specific evidence to directly guide the round-up feature.
limitations: purely theoretical with no empirical data or product context
does not address consumer financial or fintech settings
relevance_reason: General optimal-default theory that is too abstract and off-domain to directly move either design decision.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll-deduction short-term (liquid, anytime-withdrawable) savings account at five UK firms saw take-up of no more than 0.7% of eligible employees, though among those who activated, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction short-term savings program at five UK firms, tracked over the first 12 months post-activation.
why_it_matters: The closest available analog to our liquid round-up product: shows opt-in alone yields near-zero enrolment despite strong retention among the few who opt in, arguing against relying on pure opt-in if broad enrolment matters, while showing persistence isn't inherently a problem once someone actively chooses.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction channel, not direct-to-consumer app enrolment
no opt-out or active-choice comparison condition tested
relevance_reason: Closest analog on opt-in take-up and persistence for a liquid, withdrawable savings product, directly informative for the entry-design decision.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish savings observations, automatic employer contributions raised wealth accumulation far more than tax subsidies requiring active choice — each $1 of subsidy spending raised saving by only 1 cent, since 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic defaults, while the wealthier, more sophisticated 15% are 'active savers.'
methodology: Population-level administrative panel analysis of Danish retirement savings comparing active-choice subsidy programs to passive automatic-contribution policies.
why_it_matters: Foundational evidence for why passive defaults outperform active-choice mechanisms and, crucially, documents who is helped (unsophisticated passive savers) versus who self-directs regardless — directly relevant to the brief's distributional question, even though set in Danish retirement accounts.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged accounts, not a liquid consumer round-up product
predates the fintech app and current EU consumer-protection climate the brief flags as relevant
relevance_reason: The classic large-scale demonstration that passive defaults dominate active-choice mechanisms and who benefits from each, the foundational distributional evidence current work responds to.

key_finding: Introduces and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' (highlighting losses in the non-preferred option) as an alternative to automatic enrollment, recommending it as a complement or substitute when opt-out defaults are infeasible or unethical.
methodology: Narrative review plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against status-quo/default framings; abstract-only, primarily in a medication-adherence context.
why_it_matters: This is the originating paper on the exact technique — active/enhanced active choice as an enrollment design — that the brief's Decision 1 is choosing between; it directly informs whether active choice can substitute for opt-out without the same ethical/manipulation exposure.
limitations: field experiments are in health/medication-adherence settings, not consumer financial products
no reported persistence or amount-saved outcomes at 6-12 months
abstract gives no effect sizes for the active-choice comparison
outside the recency window; predates app-based fintech and EU dark-pattern scrutiny
relevance_reason: Directly originates and tests the active-choice design that is one of the two enrollment options the brief is deciding between, making it foundational to the C6 comparison even though its empirical setting is health care rather than consumer finance.

key_finding: A randomized reminder nudge in a Brazilian financial-management platform cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised checking-account overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Field experiment (randomized intervention) with a consumer financial-management platform, tracking downstream fee outcomes across linked accounts.
why_it_matters: Shows concretely that a consumer-facing financial nudge can help most users while making a vulnerable subgroup worse off — exactly the distributional risk the brief flags for round-up defaults, and a template for the kind of heterogeneity analysis the team should run before declaring the feature a success.
limitations: studies a payment reminder, not an enrollment default or contribution-level anchor
no measure of enrollment or opt-out behavior, so C1/C6 don't transfer directly
single-market (Brazil) platform; EU regulatory context not addressed
relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed fintech field experiment showing that a well-intentioned nudge can help the average user while harming an identifiable subgroup — direct evidence for the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' concern (C5), in the right kind of setting (C4).
